sources.title: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa 3.17
sources.edition: Desiraju Hanumanta Rao prose translation; site chapter numbering; commentary interspersed
sources.locator: 3.17, narrative vv. 10, 16, 23–24 (site prose; verse numbering follows the corresponding Sanskrit text)

claims.subject: rama
claims.summary: While Rāma is at the Pañcavaṭī hermitage with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā arrives and addresses him.
claims.speaker: Narrator
claims.note: The meeting occurs downstream of the Agastya-to-Pañcavaṭī direction; this passage does not depict Śūrpaṇakhā meeting Agastya.

claims.subject: shurpanakha
claims.summary: The narrator identifies Śūrpaṇakhā as Rāvaṇa's sister, and she names Rāvaṇa as her brother.
claims.speaker: Narrator; Śūrpaṇakhā
claims.note: Directly stated in the narrative and her self-introduction.

claims.subject: ravana_epic
claims.summary: Śūrpaṇakhā describes Rāvaṇa as the son of Viśravas.
claims.speaker: Śūrpaṇakhā
claims.note: A lineage statement attributed to Śūrpaṇakhā in this Rāmāyaṇa witness.

claims.subject: shurpanakha
claims.summary: Śūrpaṇakhā names Kumbhakarṇa as her brother.
claims.speaker: Śūrpaṇakhā
claims.note: Her description that he sleeps profoundly is not encoded as an identity or kinship claim.

claims.subject: shurpanakha
claims.summary: Śūrpaṇakhā names Vibhīṣaṇa as her brother and says that he does not behave like a demon.
claims.speaker: Śūrpaṇakhā
claims.note: The characterization is retained as her speech, without importing later narrative framing.

claims.subject: shurpanakha
claims.summary: Śūrpaṇakhā names Khara among her brothers.
claims.speaker: Śūrpaṇakhā
claims.note: Her next reference identifies Dūṣaṇa as the other of the two named brothers.

claims.subject: shurpanakha
claims.summary: Śūrpaṇakhā names Dūṣaṇa alongside Khara as one of her two brothers renowned for bravery in war.
claims.speaker: Śūrpaṇakhā
claims.note: The passage explicitly introduces the pair as her brothers.

search_log.outcome: Compared GRETIL text listings, its Mahābhārata archive record, the INDOLOGY Virtual e-Text Archive, and current GRETIL mirror documentation. See notes for corpus path and reuse caveat.

notes: The additions form a source-linked chain outward from existing graph material: Agastya directs Rāma toward Pañcavaṭī (already represented), and Rāmāyaṇa 3.17 places Rāma at the hermitage when he meets Śūrpaṇakhā; her speech supplies the sibling and parent links. No direct Agastya–Śūrpaṇakhā encounter is claimed.

For scalable Sanskrit text discovery, GRETIL is the strongest practical starting point: https://gretil.sub.uni-goettingen.de/gretil.html lists the Tokunaga/John Smith machine-readable Mahābhārata by parvan in UTF-8 files and the Rāmāyaṇa in TEI XML plus plain/analytic transformations. The current mirror documents downloadable files at https://github.com/INDOLOGY/GRETIL-mirror; Mahābhārata is the exception to the mirror's TEI/XML corpus layer, so its downloadable parvan text files are the relevant form. A snapshot is catalogued at https://zenodo.org/records/6467313. The Rāmāyaṇa listing includes Tokunaga/Smith editions and a Southern recension; pin edition/recension before comparing names or locators.

GRETIL is an index/archive of e-texts with multiple contributors, not one blanket open-license corpus. Treat the ancient Sanskrit text and modern transcription, edition, encoding, markup, and translations separately; inspect each file's provenance and reuse terms before redistribution or commercial use. For machine-readable searchable breadth rather than critical-edition authority, the INDOLOGY Virtual e-Text Archive also links distributed text files: https://indology.info/virtual-e-text-archive-of-indic-texts/. For Ramayana's Baroda Critical Edition-based machine text provenance, see https://sanskritdocuments.org/mirrors/ramayana/valmiki/ramayana.htm; GRETIL is useful for scalable retrieval, while passage claims should still be checked against a declared edition and exact locator.
